notes.meaning: Israel looks back on a long history of suffering and invites the whole nation to join in this song. The nation's youth points all the way back to their earliest days, when they were enslaved in Egypt. From the very beginning of their story, enemies have repeatedly tried to destroy them.

The song repeats the painful truth that enemies attacked again and again, but immediately adds a shout of victory. Those who hated God's people were never able to wipe them out completely. God protected his nation so that their enemies could not win in the end.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church father Augustine taught that enemies could not prevail because a godly person refuses to consent to their evil ways.

notes.meaning: The suffering of God's people was so severe that it felt like an ox team dragging a plow across someone's bare back. This word picture describes deep, cruel wounds and harsh slavery, like earth cut open by long furrows. It shows how ruthlessly Israel's captors treated them without showing any pity.

The Lord showed his righteousness by stepping in to rescue his people. Righteousness here means that God was faithful and kept his promise to save them. He cut through the ropes and harness that tied them to their oppressors' plow, setting them completely free from captivity.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Following an ancient Latin translation, Augustine understood the cut cords as God cutting the necks of proud sinners who refuse to confess their sins.

notes.meaning: The writer asks God to turn back everyone who hates Zion, sending them away in defeat and shame. Zion was the holy hill in Jerusalem where God dwelt with his people, so hating Zion meant hating God himself. Those who set themselves against God's kingdom will eventually see all their evil plans fail.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic theologian Robert Bellarmine suggested this prayer could ask for a good kind of shame that leads enemies to repent and turn to God, as the apostle Paul did.

notes.meaning: The enemies of God are compared to weeds sprouting on flat, dirt-plastered rooftops. Because the dirt on a roof is very thin, the seeds have no deep roots and scorch in the hot sun before they can even grow up. In the same way, the proud schemes of the wicked may shoot up fast, but they will quickly dry up and vanish.

A real field produces a rich crop that workers can cut and gather into large bundles. Rooftop grass is so weak and useless that a reaper cannot even grab a single handful of it. Those who harm God's people will end up with nothing to show for all their hard work.

In Bible times, travelers walking past a harvest field would call out a blessing from the Lord, and the reapers would warmly bless them back. The useless weeds of the wicked will never receive such a happy greeting, because there will be no harvest to celebrate. God's people must never cheer on wicked plans or wish God's blessing on evil deeds.
